rows.evidence: Q1: Methodology and Optimization Results sections <U+2013> the authors generate their own five-member CWRF ensemble forecasts driven by reanalysis for 2002<U+2013>2006, bias-correct them against observed station data, and run a SWAP-based simulation-optimization of daily irrigation decisions for the Havana Lowlands, Illinois, reporting water use and profit under several forecast scenarios (Figs. 6<U+2013>9).
rows.notes: The study does report, as a model output, that reanalysis-based RCM forecasts in the optimization give about 1<U+2013>3% expected profit gain and 4<U+2013>6% irrigation water reduction relative to a no-rain baseline (Fig. 8, Conclusions), which matches the numbers in the passage. However, the water-saving and profit results are purely simulation-optimization outputs: the SWAP crop model was calibrated in earlier work (Wang and Cai 2007) and nothing in this paper compares simulated irrigation amounts, yields or profits with measured values from the real farms. Only the forecast inputs (six weather variables) are compared with observations (bias correction, skill scores in Figs. 2<U+2013>5). Under the rule that a model counts only when its output is checked against measurements of the real system, Q2 is rated no; the doubt is noted here because the model is driven by observed historical weather and a previously calibrated crop model. The authors themselves stress the result is an upper limit because reanalysis, not operational forecasts, drives the RCM, and they report large ensemble uncertainty (Figs. 10<U+2013>12), but these cannot be credited once Q2 is no. The passage's mention of ETo forecasts is slightly inaccurate: the study forecasts rainfall and min/max temperature and replaces humidity, wind and radiation with climatology.

notes: Full text available; figure contents are not visible but their captions and the text describing them are. Single case-study site (Havana Lowlands, Mason County, Illinois), one crop (corn), five seasons, one calibrated field-scale SWAP model.
